newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Trade growth slipped to four pct in 1996-WTO.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Trade growth slipped to four pct in 1996-WTO.

text.p: Growth in world goods trade, hit by a slowdown in major Asian economies and continuing low demand in Western Europe, dropped to four per cent last year from eight per cent in 1995, an official report said on Thursday.

But, in its annual review of global figures, the World Trade Organisation (WTO) predicted a modest increase over the 1996 performance this year if an expected overall recovery in the two key regions was confirmed.

And the report found Latin America, with a growth in export volume of 11 per cent, led by a strong 20 per cent surge from Mexico, and North America -- the United States and Canada -- with 5.5 per cent, running well ahead of the global average.

The study, based on preliminary figures, described Asia's export growth of only 2.5 per cent as the surprising feature of 1996. It was the lowest among world regions and was well down on the five per cent output growth for the Asian area.
Around the world, trade growth has consistently outpaced output growth over the past decade.
But WTO chief economist Richard Blackhurst told a news briefing he saw the decline in Asia as cyclical. "I see no fundamental change in Asian economies that would have caused it," he added.

The global growth percentage was three per cent lower than that predicted by the WTO early last year and one per cent down on a forecast it issued last December at its first-ever ministerial meeting in Singapore.

Also down was the growth rate of the U.S. dollar value of trade in commercial services -- from banking and insurance to transport and tourism -- which dropped to about five per cent from 14 per cent in 1995.

Compiled by WTO economic analysts, the report noted that last year's growth in goods trade volume was in line with the average for the first four years of the decade and followed two strong years with a peak at 10 per cent in 1994.

"A modest increase in trade growth is expected this year, based largely on the projected recovery of economic growth and trade in Western Europe and Asia, and continued high growth in Latin America," it said.

The report recorded that overall trade growth was still running well ahead of world goods output or gross domestic product -- 2.5 per cent last year -- as it has consistently done since the mid-1980s, underlining continuing integration of the global economy.
Western European import demand remained sluggish, growing at only three per cent from six per cent in 1995 and below the global average for the fifth year in a row, it said.
Against this background, it was Asia's surprise export growth decline from over 9.5 per cent in 1995 to 2.5 per cent that had played a major part in the downswing, the study indicated.

Blackhurst said there was still no full explanation for the Asian decline but suggested one reason was a sharp drop in world demand for office and telecommunications equipment, which in 1995 accounted for some 23 per cent of Asian exports.

In value terms, according to the report, global exports had topped the $5,000 billion ($2.9 trillion) level for the first time, touching $5,100 billion by the end of December, a figure which also marked a four per cent increase on 1995.

This compared with 20 per cent value growth in 1995 over 1994 but much of the relative decline was accounted for by the appreciation of the U.S. dollar in 1996 against other major currencies, the WTO said.

In terms of value, the United States remained the world's number one individual exporter, with a nearly 12 per cent share of the global total of $5,100 billion, and the top importer, with just over 15 per cent.

But with figures for all its 15 members counted together, the European Union was the top exporting power while, excluding trade among its members, it remained the second importer after the United States. ($1= 1.722 German Marks)
